analysis.one_liner: Lets health insurers again put annual dollar caps on the benefits they will pay.
analysis.headline: A single representative's bill to let insurers cap yearly health benefits was introduced in November 2010, sent to committee, and never got a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal one piece of the 2010 health care law: the rule that stops health plans from setting an annual dollar limit on how much they will pay for a person's care. If it had passed, an insurer could again cut off payment for a seriously ill patient once a yearly cap was reached, leaving the patient to pay the rest out of pocket. The bill was introduced by one New York Democrat with no cosponsors on November 29, 2010, and was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it stayed until the two-year Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers benefit if the bill passes, because they regain the power to limit their total payout for any one person to a fixed annual dollar amount, controlling their costs on expensive cases. Employers that sponsor group plans would also gain flexibility to cap their own exposure to large claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health insurers and large group plans

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Affordable Care Act's prohibition on annual limits on the dollar value of benefits, restoring insurers' ability to cap yearly payouts under group and individual plans.
The repeal takes effect on the date of enactment, so caps could be reinstated immediately.

analysis.who_pays: Patients with serious or chronic conditions pay. Once a plan hits its annual cap, the patient bears the full cost of continued care out of pocket, and the ACA's ban on annual limits was designed specifically to stop people from running out of coverage mid-illness.

drawbacks.text: Restoring annual limits would expose seriously ill people to unlimited out-of-pocket costs once their cap is reached, exactly the situation the Affordable Care Act provision was written to prevent.
The bill repeals the protection outright and immediately, with no replacement safeguards, transitional relief, or phase-in for people already undergoing expensive treatment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would hand insurers a cost-control tool but shift the risk of catastrophic medical bills onto the sickest patients. Given that the provision it targets is one of the Affordable Care Act's core protections against running out of coverage mid-illness, the cost to patients appears far larger than the insurer convenience gained.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gary Ackerman (D-NY) introduced the bill on November 29, 2010, in the final weeks of the 111th Congress.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction and received no further action.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, so the bill died in committee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients and the public are better off, since the ACA's protection against annual benefit caps remained untouched. Health insurers are worse off only in that they did not regain the ability to cap payouts, but nothing was lost that they had. The bill also reads as symbolic messaging; it was titled to argue the ACA could not be repealed outright and picked a single provision to target.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, and the bill had zero cosponsors from either party, so no positional split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would restore insurers' ability to set annual dollar caps on benefits, limiting their payout on the most expensive cases. The cost of that cap falls on patients who exhaust it mid-treatment, so the industry's gain runs against patients' interests.
